course.title: First Aid
course.description: What to do, and in what order, in the first minutes of an emergency: scene safety, the primary survey, CPR and AED, choking, bleeding, burns, fractures, head injury, heart attack, stroke, allergic reactions, poisoning and heat or cold. This course teaches the knowledge; it does not replace hands-on training with a certified instructor.
course.audience: A capable adult with no medical training who wants to know what a first aider does and why, before or alongside a hands-on course. They need only everyday knowledge of the body. Nothing here qualifies the learner to give first aid in a workplace or to hold a certificate.

paragraphs: The European Resuscitation Council states that each minute of delay before a person in cardiac arrest receives a shock from a defibrillator reduces their probability of survival by 10%. The help a person receives in those minutes, before professionals arrive, is first aid, and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies gives it three aims: to alleviate suffering, to prevent further illness or injury and to promote recovery. None of them asks you to diagnose or cure anything, only to recognise what is happening and to act on it until someone who can treat the cause takes over.

Most of first aid comes down to a few decisions made quickly and in the right order, and each one rests on a reason you can understand. A person who is unresponsive and gasping is treated as being in cardiac arrest, because the gasps of the first minutes after the heart stops are easily mistaken for breathing, and a burn is held under running water for many minutes, because the heat goes on damaging the layers of the skin after the source has been removed. Knowing the reason behind a step lets you apply it to a case that does not look exactly like the one you learned.

The guidance comes from bodies such as the IFRC, the European Resuscitation Council and the American Heart Association, which all revised their guidelines in 2025 and still differ on a few details, such as how they state the depth of chest compressions or when to make the emergency call, so national courses teach slightly different versions. Reading about first aid is not a substitute for a practical course, where compressions, back blows and the recovery position are learned with an instructor, and in a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.
outcomes: You'll be able to make a scene safe, call for help with the information a dispatcher needs, and carry out a primary survey in the right order.
You'll be able to state the adult CPR figures (where to press, how fast, how deep, and the compression-to-breath ratio) and the steps for using an AED.
You'll be able to tell mild from severe choking and give the right sequence for each.
You'll be able to control severe bleeding, treat a burn, and support a suspected fracture or head injury without making it worse.
You'll be able to recognise a heart attack, a stroke, anaphylaxis, poisoning, heat stroke and hypothermia, and say what to do and what to avoid.

concepts.title: Aims of first aid
concepts.summary: To preserve life, to prevent the condition worsening and to promote recovery, until professional help takes over.

concepts.title: Scene safety
concepts.summary: A first aider checks for danger to themselves, the casualty and bystanders before approaching, because a second casualty helps no one.

concepts.title: Calling for help
concepts.summary: The call to the local emergency number gives the exact location, what happened, how many people are hurt and their state, and the dispatcher's instructions are followed.

concepts.title: Limits of this course
concepts.summary: Reading a guideline is not training; hands-on practice with a certified instructor is how skills like CPR are learned and kept.

concepts.title: Primary survey
concepts.summary: A quick ordered check for life-threatening problems: danger, response, airway, breathing, severe bleeding.

concepts.title: Response check
concepts.summary: Speak loudly, tap the shoulders; no response means the person is unresponsive.

concepts.title: Normal breathing
concepts.summary: Look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds; occasional gasps are not normal breathing.

concepts.title: Opening the airway
concepts.summary: Tilting the head back and lifting the chin lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat.

concepts.title: Recovery position
concepts.summary: Lying on the side with the head tilted back and the mouth angled down so that fluid drains and the tongue cannot block the airway.

concepts.title: When to use it
concepts.summary: For an unresponsive person who is breathing normally and has no suspected injury that forbids moving them.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest
concepts.summary: The heart stops pumping effectively, so the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

concepts.title: Chest compressions
concepts.summary: Pressing on the centre of the chest 100 to 120 times a minute, 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully each time.

concepts.title: Compression-to-breath ratio
concepts.summary: A trained rescuer gives 30 compressions then 2 breaths; an untrained rescuer, or one unwilling to give breaths, gives compressions alone.

concepts.title: Minimising interruptions
concepts.summary: Blood flow to the brain stops when compressions stop, so pauses are kept as short as possible.

concepts.title: Automated external defibrillator
concepts.summary: A device that analyses the heart's rhythm and, if it finds a shockable rhythm, tells the rescuer to deliver a shock.

concepts.title: Shockable rhythm
concepts.summary: A chaotic or very fast rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) that a shock can stop so the heart may restart normally.

concepts.title: Pad placement
concepts.summary: Two adhesive pads go on bare, dry skin in the positions shown on the pads.

concepts.title: Different causes
concepts.summary: Children and infants more often stop breathing first, because of choking, drowning or illness, so breaths matter more.

concepts.title: Scaled compressions
concepts.summary: Compress the chest by about one third of its depth, at the same rate as for an adult.

concepts.title: Infant technique
concepts.summary: The rescuer uses the technique the cited guideline gives for infants (two thumbs encircling the chest or two fingers; writer must confirm the technique and the child ratio for the edition used).

concepts.title: Mild choking
concepts.summary: The person can speak, cough and breathe; encourage them to keep coughing.

concepts.title: Severe choking
concepts.summary: The person cannot speak, cough effectively or breathe, may clutch the throat and goes silent.

concepts.title: Back blows and thrusts
concepts.summary: For an adult with severe choking give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, and alternate; for an infant use back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

concepts.title: Direct pressure
concepts.summary: Firm, continuous pressure on the wound with a pad or the hands, kept on until help arrives.

concepts.title: Tourniquet
concepts.summary: A band tightened above a bleeding limb wound when direct pressure cannot control life-threatening bleeding; the time is noted and it is not loosened.

concepts.title: Shock
concepts.summary: Failure of circulation to deliver enough blood to the body, shown by pale, cold, clammy skin, fast breathing and pulse, weakness and confusion.

concepts.title: Cooling
concepts.summary: Cool a thermal burn promptly with cool running water for the time the guideline gives, to reduce damage and pain.

concepts.title: Dressing
concepts.summary: Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy, non-sticking dressing or cling film applied lengthways.

concepts.title: Burns needing urgent help
concepts.summary: Burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, in infants, or caused by chemicals or electricity need urgent medical care.

concepts.title: Fracture
concepts.summary: A broken bone; signs include pain, swelling, deformity, bruising and inability to use the part.

concepts.title: Immobilising
concepts.summary: Supporting the injured part in the position found, using padding, a sling or a splint, to reduce pain and further damage.

concepts.title: Open fracture
concepts.summary: A fracture with a wound where the bone may show; control bleeding and cover the wound without pressing on the bone.

concepts.title: Concussion
concepts.summary: A temporary disturbance of brain function after a blow, with headache, confusion, memory loss or dizziness.

concepts.title: Red flags
concepts.summary: Loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, drowsiness, seizure, weakness or clear fluid from the nose or ears mean urgent medical care.

concepts.title: Spinal precautions
concepts.summary: With a suspected spine injury, keep the head and body still unless the person is in danger or cannot keep an open airway.

concepts.title: Heart attack
concepts.summary: A blocked coronary artery starves heart muscle of blood, causing chest pain or pressure that may spread to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating and breathlessness.

concepts.title: Stroke
concepts.summary: An interruption of blood to part of the brain, from a blockage or a bleed.

concepts.title: FAST
concepts.summary: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call the emergency number.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis
concepts.summary: A severe, rapid allergic reaction that can narrow the airway and drop blood pressure.

concepts.title: Adrenaline auto-injector
concepts.summary: A pen that injects adrenaline into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed, held in place for the time on its instructions.

concepts.title: Poison information
concepts.summary: A poison centre or emergency service gives advice that depends on the substance, the amount and the time.

concepts.title: Heat exhaustion
concepts.summary: Heavy sweating, weakness and headache in the heat; treated by moving to a cool place, resting and drinking fluids.

concepts.title: Heat stroke
concepts.summary: A medical emergency with very high body temperature and confusion or collapse; cool the person quickly and call the emergency number.

concepts.title: Hypothermia
concepts.summary: A body temperature low enough to impair function, with shivering, confusion and drowsiness; prevent further heat loss and handle gently.

lessons.title: What a first aider does, and where it stops
lessons.orientation: Name the aims of first aid, find the dangers at a scene, and build an emergency call.

lead.text: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies defines **first aid** as the immediate assistance provided to an ill or injured person until professional help arrives. Its 2025 guidelines add that first aid interventions seek to *alleviate suffering, prevent further illness or injury and promote recovery*.
A first aider keeps the person alive, stops the problem getting worse and makes them as comfortable as possible, and then hands over to ambulance crews or doctors who can treat the cause.

afterFigure.text: The same document describes a first aid provider as someone who recognises their own limits and seeks additional care when needed.

reveal.text: Alleviating suffering, preventing further illness or injury and promoting recovery make three aims, and none of them is a cure.
The next screen shows the road from above, with the dangers a first aider should find first.

lead.text: The IFRC general approach starts with **scene assessment**: look for fire, exposed electrical wires, traffic, water, confined spaces with poisonous gas and any violence, and look for the areas that are safe or have fewer dangers.

If the danger can be removed, remove it, for example by stopping traffic or switching off power. If it cannot, *do not approach*: call for help, or give help from a distance, and give your own safety priority.

reveal.text: Carbon monoxide has no smell, so a closed space with an engine running looks harmless until you are in it. People with breathing equipment go in; you call.

lead.text: A **dispatcher** is the trained person who answers the emergency number and sends the right help. The figure splits an example call into four parts: where you are, what happened, how many people are hurt and what state they are in, and what you have already done.

Where life-saving care is under way, make the call on the phone's speaker function so that you can help at the same time. IFRC also says it can be better to call early with incomplete information than to wait until you know everything, and the ERC says dispatchers give clear step-by-step instructions, including for CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

afterFigure.text: The number you dial depends on where you are. The British Red Cross teaches 999, the American Red Cross 9-1-1, and the European Resuscitation Council gives 112 for Europe, or the local number, so find out the one for your own country now.

steps.headline: Listen to how the example call is built, one line at a time.

workedSteps.text: The caller starts with the place, so that help is already on its way before anything else is said.
workedSteps.math: I am at 14 Mill Road, outside the library.

workedSteps.text: Next comes what happened, in one plain sentence.
workedSteps.math: A man of about 60 collapsed and is not responding.

workedSteps.text: The caller adds one more line before saying what they are doing.
Last, what the caller is doing now. The dispatcher takes it from here and may coach the caller.

reveal.text: Putting the phone on speaker lets the dispatcher hear and guide while your hands work.

lead.text: The IFRC guidelines call themselves "a foundation, not a curriculum or training package". This course explains what a first aider does and why, and it cannot replace a hands-on course, because the force, rhythm and feel of CPR are learned on a manikin with an instructor who watches and corrects you.

Where guidance differs between countries, the lessons name both versions instead of choosing one for you. The ERC says that courses should explain local Good Samaritan laws, which protect people who help in good faith, and duty-to-respond laws, both of which vary from place to place, and this course gives no legal advice.

afterFigure.text: Look for an accredited course near you, which also teaches the local emergency number and the local law.

blocks.text: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies defines first aid as the immediate assistance given to an ill or injured person until professional help arrives, and its 2025 guidelines give that assistance three aims: to alleviate suffering, to prevent further illness or injury and to promote recovery. None of the three is a cure, so a first aider keeps the person safe and stable and leaves the treatment of the cause to whoever takes over.
Within that limit there is a good deal to get right in the first minute, and the order in which it is done matters.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the aims of first aid, check a scene for danger, and give a dispatcher the four things they need.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: A first aider checks the scene for danger first, calls the emergency number with the location, what happened, how many people are hurt and what has been done, and then helps within the limits of what they know.

blocks.text: You saw that first aid aims to relieve suffering, stop things getting worse and help recovery, and that the first move is to look for hazards instead of rushing in. The call to the emergency number follows the same order each time, and the dispatcher can coach you through what comes next.
Numbers and some rules differ between countries and between guideline bodies, so keep the national guidance for where you live alongside this course, and add a hands-on course for the skills.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the first check on the person: whether they respond, whether their airway is open and whether they are breathing normally.

lessons.title: The primary survey
lessons.orientation: Carry out the response, airway, breathing and bleeding checks in order.

lead.text: The IFRC guidelines ask the first aider to look for life-threatening problems in a fixed order, a check often called the **primary survey** or the ABC check. It asks whether the person responds, whether the airway is open and clear, whether they are breathing normally and whether they are bleeding severely.

To check for a response you gently shake the person's shoulders and speak loudly and clearly, asking something like "Are you alright?". A person who does not move or react to noise or touch is **unresponsive**. If they do respond, the general approach continues and you ask what happened. If they do not, you shout for help and the next two checks follow.

afterFigure.text: Each check decides what comes next, and a person who answers you is talking, which shows their airway is open and they are breathing.

reveal.text: The next screen explains why a gasp is not a breath.

lead.text: First the airway is opened. In an unresponsive person the muscles relax and the tongue can fall back and block the throat, so you tilt the head back, lifting the chin, which pulls the tongue forward. The figure shows what follows. With the airway open, you **look, listen and feel** for normal breathing for up to ten seconds: look for movement of the chest or abdomen, listen for breath sounds and feel for air on your cheek.

IFRC describes normal breathing as air moving at an even pace without irregular sounds such as gurgling. In the first minutes after cardiac arrest a person may show **agonal breathing**, an irregular and laboured pattern or noisy gasping. It is not normal, and IFRC's rule is that if there is any doubt, you assume the breathing is not normal.

afterFigure.text: A short period of seizure-like movement can also occur at the start of a cardiac arrest, and the ERC adds that people who collapse during hard exercise may seem to be breathing heavily with their eyes open. In both cases the guidance is to check the breathing once the movement stops, and to start CPR if it is not normal.

reveal.text: Ten seconds keeps the check short. If you cannot tell, you do not keep waiting; you treat the breathing as not normal.

steps.headline: A man on a pavement does not answer when spoken to or tapped.

workedSteps.text: You check that it is safe to reach him, then speak loudly and tap his shoulders. He does not react.
You shout for help, ask someone to call the emergency number, and tilt his head back, lifting the chin.
You look at his chest, listen and feel for ten seconds and hear only occasional snoring gasps.
Breathing is not normal, so the next step follows at once.

reveal.text: The movement stops, the runner lies still, and the guidance says the check continues exactly as before.

lead.text: For a lay rescuer, response and breathing are the signs to go by. IFRC says taking the pulse as the only sign of cardiac arrest is unreliable, and all the organisations it reviewed recommend starting CPR for the general public without a pulse check. Bleeding that is severe can be treated at any point in the survey.

Guidance differs a little on when to call. The ERC emphasises calling early, before assessing breathing, if the person is unresponsive, and the American Heart Association recommends calling once cardiac arrest is recognised. In this course, the call is made as soon as the person is unresponsive and you can do it without delay.

lessons.nextAction: Decide when to use the recovery position and describe how it keeps the airway open.

blocks.text: When the heart stops pumping blood, the IFRC guidelines say, the person quickly becomes unresponsive and their breathing becomes abnormal or stops altogether. Neither sign needs any equipment to find, so a first aider can recognise a cardiac arrest within seconds by speaking to the person, touching them and checking how they breathe.
Those checks are made in a fixed order called the **primary survey**, and its answers tell you whether the person needs to lie on their side, needs CPR or needs pressure on a wound.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to carry out the primary survey in order and say when breathing counts as not normal.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: The primary survey checks response, airway, breathing and severe bleeding in order, and breathing that is not steady and even is treated as not normal.

blocks.text: You saw that a person who does not respond has their airway opened by tilting the head and lifting the chin, and that you look, listen and feel for no more than ten seconds. Gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest and not of breathing, and lay rescuers do not wait for a pulse.
Normal breathing leads to the recovery position and abnormal breathing leads to CPR.

lessons.title: Unresponsive and breathing: the recovery position
lessons.orientation: Choose the recovery position or CPR from the breathing check, and describe how to do the position.

reveal.text: Lying on the side is the shape the recovery position gives. The next screen explains why it keeps the airway open.

lead.text: IFRC's remedy for a person who is unresponsive and **breathing normally** is to maintain an open airway by moving them onto their side and tilting their head back. This is called the **recovery position**.

The British Red Cross explains why the position works: with the head back, the tongue falls forward, and blood or vomit can drain out of the mouth instead of being breathed in. A person who is unresponsive and breathing normally may still have a serious condition, so you should always call the emergency services.

If breathing is normal, the recovery position keeps the airway open while help comes. If it is not normal, the person is treated as being in cardiac arrest and lies flat on their back for CPR. The ERC says in terms that the recovery position is not for abnormal breathing or trauma.

A suspected spine injury is the case where guidance differs, and the figure marks it. IFRC says to avoid moving someone with a suspected traumatic spinal injury if help will arrive soon, and to keep the airway open with head tilt and chin lift or a jaw thrust, pushing the lower jaw forward from behind its angles, since that may move the neck less. The British Red Cross says to turn them onto their side anyway, keeping the spine in a straight line and using a helper if there is one. IFRC allows turning them with the spine kept in line when help is far away and more than one first aider is present.

afterFigure.text: Both sources agree that breathing is the priority, and a hands-on course in your country will teach the version that your authorities use.

reveal.text: Noisy gasps count as abnormal breathing, which is the cue to start CPR on their back.

lead.text: The St John Ambulance sequence, reviewed in April 2025, begins with you kneeling beside the person and straightening their legs, after taking off glasses and removing bulky items from their pockets. You place the arm nearest to you at a right angle to the body with the elbow bent and the palm up, and bring the far arm across the chest so the back of the hand rests against the cheek nearest to you.

Then you pull the far knee up with the foot flat on the floor, and keeping the hand against the cheek you pull on the far leg to roll the person towards you. Adjust the top leg so it is bent at a right angle, and tilt the head back and lift the chin to keep the airway open. Call for help if that has not yet been done, and watch the person's breathing.

afterFigure.text: IFRC does not set out one fixed method, so a different course may place the hands or legs a little differently. What matters is the result: the person is on their side with the airway open. For a person who is pregnant, IFRC gives the left side as an option, because it prevents compression of the blood vessels that feed the uterus.

steps.headline: Walk through the first two moves on a person lying on their back.

workedSteps.text: Kneel beside the person and straighten their legs. Take off glasses, and remove only the bulky items you can see in the pockets.
Next comes the arm nearest to you.
Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of the hand against the cheek nearest to you.

workedSteps.text: Pull the far knee up so that the foot is flat on the floor.

reveal.text: IFRC gives this as an option that protects the blood vessels feeding the uterus. The other steps stay the same.

lead.text: The position protects the airway but it does not treat the cause of the unresponsiveness. IFRC says to monitor the person for any change in breathing or level of response, and to tell the emergency service that the person is unresponsive and breathing normally, including what you know about the cause.

If breathing changes, becomes noisy or stops, the person is back at the breathing check of the survey and CPR begins. St John Ambulance adds one practical point: if the person remains in the position for 30 minutes, you roll them onto the other side.

blocks.text: On their back, an unresponsive person's tongue can block the throat, and vomit has no way out except back down the airway, so a person whose lungs are working perfectly well can still be unable to breathe because of the way they are lying.
The IFRC guideline for a person who is unresponsive but breathing normally is to place them in a position that keeps the airway open by itself, called the **recovery position**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say when to use the recovery position, describe how it is done and say what to keep checking.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: The recovery position keeps an open airway in a person who is unresponsive and breathing normally, and it is replaced by CPR if the breathing stops being normal.

blocks.text: You saw that lying on the side lets the tongue fall forward and fluid drain, and that the position is not used for abnormal breathing. Guidance on a suspected spine injury differs between IFRC and the British Red Cross, and both put the airway first.
The four moves are near arm out, far arm and knee up, roll towards you and tilt the head, and the person is then watched until help arrives.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson covers the other branch: adult CPR, with its place, rate, depth and ratio.

lessons.title: CPR for an adult
lessons.orientation: State the figures for adult CPR and work out the time for a cycle.

lead.text: In **cardiac arrest** the heart can no longer pump blood effectively, so the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. The British Red Cross says that the chance of restarting a heart with compressions alone is very small, and that a heart usually needs an electric shock from an AED. What compressions do is push a small amount of blood around the body, which keeps the brain and heart alive until that shock can be given.

For this reason IFRC makes starting compressions the key action. It says it is unlikely that a first aider can make the situation worse by doing CPR, and that when in doubt, start, with the call made first or at the same time.

reveal.text: Ribs can break during compressions, and the guidance accepts that. Pressing too lightly gives the person less blood flow, which is the greater risk.

lead.text: IFRC places the compressions in the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone. It suggests the dominant hand goes against the breastbone and the other hand over it, with the person on a firm surface if that does not delay starting. You kneel beside the person with your shoulders directly over your hands and your arms straight, so that your body weight does the work.
The depth is about 5 cm for an adult, and IFRC says to avoid more than 6 cm. The ERC gives 5 to 6 cm and the American Red Cross at least 2 inches, which is about 5 cm.

reveal.text: The target is about 5 cm and the limit is 6 cm, so the range is narrow, and the next screen turns to speed.

lead.text: The rate is 100 to 120 compressions a minute, which IFRC, the ERC and the American Red Cross all give. The British Red Cross puts it as two pushes a second.

Between compressions you let the chest come **fully back up**, which is called recoil. IFRC says to avoid leaning on the chest, because the heart can only refill with blood if the pressure is released.

diagram.alt: Three rows of tick marks showing how many compressions fit into ten seconds at 100, 110 and 120 compressions per minute. One row is highlighted at a time.
diagram.caption: Each tick is one compression. Use the buttons to compare the rates.

reveal.text: The range is 100 to 120 a minute for adults, children and babies alike.

lead.text: IFRC says that a first aider who is trained, able and willing can combine chest compressions with rescue breaths at a ratio of **30:2**, meaning 30 compressions followed by two breaths. Each breath takes about one second and should make the chest visibly rise, and the two breaths together should interrupt compressions for less than ten seconds.

If you are unable or unwilling to give breaths, you continue with compressions alone, which the ERC calls an acceptable approach. Breaths may be particularly helpful when the cause is a lack of oxygen, such as drowning or choking, and where a defibrillator will be some time coming.

afterFigure.text: In every case the aim is to keep the pauses short, because blood flow to the brain stops when compressions stop.

steps.headline: Work out how long one set of 30 compressions takes at the fastest rate in the range.

workedSteps.text: The rate is 120 compressions a minute, so 30 compressions are 30 / 120 of a minute.
Convert that to seconds, multiplying by 60.
At the slowest rate, 100 a minute, the same calculation uses 30 / 100 in place of 30 / 120, so the set takes a few seconds longer.
The two breaths add at most 10 seconds, so at 120 a minute one 30:2 cycle lasts at most 25 seconds.

reveal.text: Real CPR has pauses for breaths and shocks, which is why the count in practice is lower and why every pause is kept short.
The guidance wants this rescuer to start and carry on rather than stop.

lead.text: IFRC says to continue until you are told to pause by a defibrillator or a professional responder, or until the person shows signs of recovery, which are coughing, opening the eyes, speaking, moving purposefully and breathing normally. If two or more people are present they alternate every two minutes, making sure compressions are not interrupted as the next person takes over.
Only practice with an instructor and a manikin teaches the force and rhythm, and you should find an accredited course near you.

blocks.text: Chest compressions seldom restart a heart, which usually needs an electric shock from an automated external defibrillator. IFRC nevertheless makes compressions the key action for cardiac arrest: start them immediately and call the emergency services.
Compressions push a small amount of blood to the brain and heart and so keep both alive until the shock or the ambulance arrives, but only for as long as they continue and only if they are done well.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state where to press, the rate and depth, and the 30:2 ratio, and work out how long a cycle takes.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: Adult CPR presses the centre of the chest 100 to 120 times a minute, to about 5 cm and no more than 6 cm, with full recoil, in sets of 30 compressions and two breaths or in compressions alone.

blocks.text: You saw that compressions keep a little blood moving until a shock or help arrives, and that the sources agree on rate and ratio and state the depth slightly differently. At 100 to 120 a minute, 30 compressions take 15 to 18 seconds.
Every pause costs the brain blood, so breaths and shocks are kept brief and the rescuers swap every two minutes.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson adds the AED, the device that gives the shock which compressions alone rarely provide.

lessons.title: Using an AED
lessons.orientation: Put the AED steps in order and say what the device does.

reveal.text: A shock is for certain rhythms only, and CPR carries on in all the others.

lead.text: An **automated external defibrillator**, or AED, is a portable device that analyses the heart's rhythm and, if it finds a rhythm a shock can treat, delivers or tells you to deliver an electric shock.

The device cannot shock someone in error: IFRC says it will only shock when needed and never shocks a healthy heart. A shock does not always restart the heart, and it treats certain rhythms and not others, which is why compressions carry on whatever the device decides.

afterFigure.text: The device speaks, and in a fully automated model it shocks by itself. In a semi-automated one it tells you to press the shock button.

lead.text: IFRC begins with CPR and the call, and then a bystander is asked to bring the defibrillator. If you are alone and one is clearly visible nearby you can leave the person briefly to fetch it. Once it is there, you switch it on and follow the voice prompts, pausing CPR only when it is really needed. The pads go on the bare chest where the pictures on them show, and it does not matter if they are the wrong way round.

When the device analyses, and again before a shock, make sure that nobody is touching the person. If it says a shock is needed, warn the others and press the shock button, while a fully automated device shocks by itself. Then continue CPR unless told otherwise.

afterFigure.text: A second person can put on the pads while the first keeps pressing, and the compressions stop only at the moment the device asks.

lead.text: For adults, IFRC says that the front-and-side position is the usual first choice, with one pad below the collarbone and the other on the side of the chest below the armpit. A front-and-back position is an alternative when the first is not possible or the rescuer is trained, and the pictures on the pads show the position for the model you hold.

Pads should not overlap or touch, and they should be larger than 8 cm for adults. Chest hair may be removed quickly if that adds no more than a short delay. For a large-breasted person the pad goes beside or beneath the breast, and IFRC says that moving the bra aside is enough if the pad lands on bare skin.

steps.headline: A rescuer is pressing the chest when a bystander arrives with an AED.

workedSteps.text: The bystander switches the AED on and attaches the pads while compressions continue.
The device says that it is analysing. The rescuer lifts their hands and nobody touches the person.
The device advises a shock. The rescuer calls out, and the shock is delivered.
The rescuer acts at once, without a pulse check.

reveal.text: Placing a pad on the breast would spoil contact with the chest wall, and the guideline says to place it beside or under the breast.

lead.text: After a shock, the person may still not have a rhythm that moves blood well, and the device keeps analysing. IFRC says that even if the person recovers and breathes normally, they must be closely monitored until a professional assesses them, because their breathing may stop again.

Where public AEDs are fitted, signs and cabinets show where to find them, and IFRC and the ERC both say cabinets should not be locked. Practice with a trainer device in a course makes the prompts familiar, and a course also teaches the model in your area.

blocks.text: The European Resuscitation Council states that each minute of delay in getting to defibrillation reduces the probability of survival by 10%. Compressions keep blood moving, but the electric shock that can correct the heart's rhythm comes from a device that is increasingly kept in public places.
IFRC says that a bystander with little or no training can use an AED, because the device speaks its instructions aloud.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the AED steps in order and say what a shock does and does not do.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: An AED analyses the rhythm and shocks only when it can help, and the rescuer keeps CPR going, attaches the pads, stands clear and resumes compressions straight after a shock.

blocks.text: You saw that the device guides you by voice and cannot shock by mistake, that nobody touches the person during analysis or a shock, and that compressions resume at once. The pads go on bare skin below the collarbone and at the side of the chest, or on the front and back.
A shock treats some rhythms and not others, so CPR continues in every case until the device or a professional says otherwise.

lessons.title: Resuscitation for children and infants
lessons.orientation: Compare resuscitation for adults, children and babies and name where sources differ.

lead.text: IFRC says that cardiac arrest is less frequent in babies and children than in adults, and that it usually follows a breathing problem. A baby or child whose heart has stopped therefore has very little oxygen left in the blood, and for this reason IFRC makes rescue breaths a more important part of their CPR.

The size of the person sets the technique. IFRC treats someone who looks less than about one year old as a **baby**, someone who looks like a child as a **child**, and an adolescent or an adult by the adult guidelines. If you know adult CPR but not baby or child CPR, IFRC says you may use the adult sequence rather than do nothing.

reveal.text: The depth is scaled to the size of the chest, and the next screen gives the figures for a child and for a baby.

lead.text: For a child, IFRC gives a depth of one third of the chest, approximately 5 cm, using one hand or two depending on the size of the rescuer and the child. For a baby, it is at least one third of the chest, approximately 4 cm. The rate is 100 to 120 a minute for all ages.

For a baby, the technique is two thumbs side by side, with the other fingers encircling the chest to support the back. IFRC accepts two fingers as well, but the ERC recommends the two-thumb technique, and the American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics removed two-finger compressions in their 2025 guidance because they did not reach the right depth.

afterFigure.text: Mouth-to-mouth is used for a child, and a mouth over the baby's mouth and nose for a baby, blowing steadily for one second until the chest rises. IFRC adds that too many breaths push air into the stomach.

lead.text: IFRC's steps start with 30 compressions and then two breaths, but IFRC also says that starting with breaths or with compressions is equivalent. The ERC 2025 guidance for lay rescuers starts with five rescue breaths and then goes to 30:2. The American Red Cross starts with 30 compressions and then gives two breaths.

IFRC also notes that trained responders may use 15 compressions to two breaths, while some guidance uses 30:2 for everyone. If you are alone and cannot call hands-free, IFRC says to perform CPR for one minute before calling, and the American Red Cross says about two minutes. Your national guidance decides which of these you follow.

afterFigure.text: Where nothing else is known, any CPR is better than none, and IFRC says the most important thing is to do something.

steps.headline: Follow a lone rescuer doing CPR on an unresponsive child who is breathing abnormally.

workedSteps.text: The rescuer checks response by tapping the child's shoulders and asking loudly, then opens the airway and checks breathing for up to ten seconds.
There is no phone to put on speaker. The rescuer begins CPR, one hand on the centre of the chest, pressing about one third of its depth.
The rescuer carries on for a set time and then pauses to call for help.
After the call, CPR resumes, and the rescuer uses an AED with paediatric pads or mode when one arrives.

reveal.text: Both thumbs go on the lower half of the breastbone, and the fingers wrap round the back.
The ERC uses 25 kg, which it says is about eight years of age, as its limit for paediatric mode, and it adds that if the AED has no instructions for children you use it in standard mode.

lead.text: Babies and children are the area where guidelines differ most from one another, so the practical advice is to learn the version your own country teaches.
The call to the emergency number comes first or happens at the same time through the speaker, and the dispatcher can coach the whole sequence by phone for a baby or a child.

blocks.text: IFRC notes that cardiac arrest in a baby or child usually follows a breathing problem, such as choking, drowning or illness, whereas in an adult it usually arises in the heart itself. A child whose heart has stopped is therefore already short of oxygen, which is why IFRC makes rescue breaths a more important part of resuscitation for a baby or child than for an adult.

The compressions change as well, since the guidelines scale their depth to the size of the chest rather than giving one figure for every age, and place the hands to suit a smaller body. Knowing how the adult sequence changes lets you help a baby or a child, and IFRC adds that someone who knows only adult CPR may use it rather than do nothing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state how resuscitation differs for children and babies, and where the sources disagree.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: Children and babies get compressions scaled to about one third of the chest at the same rate as adults, with breaths that matter more because their arrests usually start with a breathing problem.

blocks.text: You saw that depth is about 5 cm for a child and about 4 cm for a baby, that a baby's compressions use two thumbs with the fingers encircling the chest, and that the rate stays at 100 to 120 a minute.
IFRC, the ERC and the American Red Cross differ on how to begin and on how long to wait before calling, which is a reason to learn your national version in a course.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to choking, where the actions differ for adults and babies, and where the person may become unresponsive.

lessons.title: Choking
lessons.orientation: Tell partial from complete choking and give the sequence for an adult and a baby.

reveal.text: Anyone who can speak and cough is moving air, and you encourage the coughing and stay with them.

lead.text: IFRC's first instruction is to ask the person: "Are you choking?". Its 2025 edition renamed the two cases. A **partial airway obstruction**, formerly mild choking, leaves the person able to speak, cough or cry, perhaps with a weak or forceful cough and high-pitched noises on breathing in. A **complete airway obstruction**, formerly severe choking, means the person cannot cough, speak, cry or breathe, may clutch the throat, and turns blue around the lips if it persists.

For a partial obstruction the guidance is to encourage coughing and watch, since the person may clear it better alone and stepping in could make things worse. They should be monitored until they improve, because a partial obstruction can become a complete one.

diagram.alt: A decision chart for choking. The first aider asks the person whether they are choking. If the person can cough, speak or cry, the obstruction is partial and the first aider encourages coughing and watches. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, the obstruction is complete and the first aider gives back blows and thrusts and calls for help.

lead.text: IFRC says to give up to five firm blows between the shoulder blades, with the person leaning forward. The British Red Cross uses the heel of the hand. If that fails, you give up to five **abdominal thrusts**: stand behind, put a fist between the ribs and the navel and pull sharply inward and upward with your other hand over it. IFRC then says to access the emergency services if the thrusts do not work, and to continue alternating back blows and thrusts until the blockage clears or the person becomes unresponsive. If the person becomes unresponsive, you start standard CPR.
For children over one year old, the British Red Cross gives the same sequence with less force.

afterFigure.text: IFRC also says that for adults and children chest thrusts, back blows and abdominal thrusts are equally effective, so the order above is a standard rather than the only workable choice.

A baby lies face up and receives chest thrusts with two thumbs.

reveal.text: The limit for each step is five, and you alternate the two steps.

steps.headline: A man at a table stops talking, clutches his throat and cannot cough.

workedSteps.text: You ask 'Are you choking?' and he nods but cannot speak, so the obstruction is complete.
You lean him well forward and strike firmly with the heel of your hand between the shoulder blades, up to five times.
If the blockage remains, you give up to five abdominal thrusts, and the emergency number is called.
You repeat the two steps in turn until it clears or he becomes unresponsive.

lead.text: For a baby, IFRC says to give up to five firm blows between the shoulder blades. The British Red Cross has the baby face down along your thigh with the head lower than the bottom. If that fails, turn the baby over, lay them along your knees and give chest thrusts with the two-thumb encircling technique, compressing the breastbone more sharply than in CPR, up to five times. IFRC says to call at once if this fails, and to alternate the steps until the blockage clears or the baby becomes unresponsive.

The 2025 American guidance gives the same alternation for infants, five back blows and five chest thrusts with no abdominal thrusts. IFRC adds that regional guidance differs on whether the chest thrusts use two thumbs or the heel of one hand.

reveal.text: The step for a baby differs from the adult's in this one place, and it is not on the abdomen.
The ERC explains why: compressions create airway pressures that may dislodge the object, and CPR continues until help arrives.

lead.text: IFRC says to remove solid material from the mouth only when you can see it, and never to sweep blindly with a finger, since that may push the object further in. It also says that suction airway clearance devices should not be used routinely.

Anyone given abdominal thrusts may have internal injuries, and part of the object can remain in the lungs, so IFRC says to access the emergency services after a complete obstruction even if the person seems fine now. After a partial obstruction, they should seek care if coughing continues, swallowing is hard or it still feels stuck.

blocks.text: IFRC's first instruction for a person who may be choking is a question: ask them whether they are choking. The question is practical, because a person who can answer, cough or cry is still moving air past the blockage, and a person who cannot is in a different and more dangerous situation.
A person who is still moving air is encouraged to keep coughing while you watch, and a person who is not needs back blows and thrusts at once.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell a partial obstruction from a complete one and give the right sequence for an adult and for a baby.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: A person who can cough and speak is encouraged to cough, and a person who cannot gets up to five back blows then up to five abdominal thrusts, with chest thrusts instead for a baby.

blocks.text: You saw that asking 'Are you choking?' decides the path, that a complete obstruction is treated by alternating blows and thrusts and by calling for help, and that a person who becomes unresponsive receives CPR.
Sources agree on the sequence and differ a little on when to call, so follow your national guidance. Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts needs a medical check.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from the airway to the blood: severe bleeding and shock.

lessons.title: Severe bleeding and shock
lessons.orientation: Control severe bleeding with pressure and recognise shock.

lead.text: Blood carries oxygen to the brain and heart, and when a lot of it is lost the circulation can fail. IFRC notes that even a cupful of blood, which is not immediately life threatening, can lead to fast deterioration if it is not stopped early. Its key action is therefore to apply **direct pressure** to the area as quickly as possible, and it names direct manual compression as the method for life-threatening external bleeding.

IFRC says not to use pressure points or ice, and to protect yourself from the blood with gloves or by covering your hands with plastic bags, bandages or clothing. The emergency service is called for all severe bleeding.

reveal.text: The next screen shows the order of the steps and where each belongs.

lead.text: The steps in IFRC's order are to ask the person to press on the wound, help them lie down, call, and then apply direct pressure yourself. If blood soaks through, put a second dressing over the first and press harder. Once the bleeding is under control you may bandage over the pads. If pressure fails on an arm or a leg, you may use a **tourniquet**, preferably a manufactured one, though IFRC allows an improvised one if it is all you have.

A tourniquet goes on a limb and nowhere else, above the wound, and if the first is ineffective IFRC says a second may be added above it. Tourniquets may cost the limb if left on too long, and once applied one stays on until the emergency service arrives. Where pressure and a tourniquet are both impractical, a haemostatic dressing, which carries a substance that helps blood clot, may be used, applied directly to the source of bleeding with pressure.

afterFigure.text: An object stuck in a wound is not removed. You press around it to steady it, since it may be acting as a plug.

reveal.text: IFRC lists it after direct pressure in its steps, and says to keep pressing on the wound after applying it.

steps.headline: A cut forearm soaks the first pad.

workedSteps.text: You press on the pad with firm, continuous pressure, with gloves or a barrier if you have them.
Blood shows through the pad. You do not remove it, and you place a second pad on top of it.
The bleeding is controlled and you bandage over the pads. If it were not, an arm wound would allow a tourniquet above the wound.
Help the person lie down and keep warm, and call the emergency number if that has not been done.

lead.text: A nosebleed without an injury is something people can often treat themselves.

reveal.text: IFRC says to pinch the soft lower third of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes, at most, and to spit blood out.
Ice is not recommended for a nosebleed. Signs of brain injury, an obviously deformed nose or blood-thinning medicine mean the emergency service.

lead.text: A person is in **shock** when the circulation fails and the organs do not receive enough blood. IFRC lists severe bleeding as the usual cause, with heart attack, severe burns, severe allergic reaction and serious infection as others. The figure lists the signs.

Care starts with treating the cause where that is possible, then laying the person on their back, calling the emergency number immediately, and keeping them warm. If it makes them feel better and there is no trauma, you may raise the legs 30 to 60 degrees. If breathing is hard, a position they find comfortable is acceptable.

afterFigure.text: IFRC's priority is to deal with the cause, such as a bleed or an allergic reaction, because shock itself comes from something else.

reveal.text: Pale, cool, clammy skin and fast breathing are the signs that the circulation is failing.
The raised legs are optional, they are for a person who feels better with them up, and they are not used after trauma such as a fall.

blocks.text: IFRC points out that even a cupful of blood can lead to fast deterioration if bleeding is not stopped early, and it names one action first: apply direct pressure to the area as quickly as possible.
When much blood is lost, the circulation can fail to supply the organs, a state called shock.

recap.keyIdea: Severe bleeding is controlled by direct pressure, with extra pads on top if blood soaks through, and a tourniquet only on a limb when pressure fails, while shock is treated by treating the cause, lying the person down and keeping them warm.

blocks.text: You saw that pads are added and never removed, that a tourniquet stays on until help arrives, and that a nosebleed is pinched for 10 to 15 minutes at most with the head leaning forward.
Shock shows in pale, cool, clammy skin and fast breathing, and the emergency number is called straight away.

lessons.title: Burns and scalds
lessons.orientation: Treat a burn with cooling and a loose cover, and decide when it needs urgent care.

reveal.text: The minimum and the ideal are separate figures in the guidance, and the next screen gives both.

lead.text: The burning process can continue in the layers of skin after the source has been removed, which is why IFRC puts cooling first. It says to cool thermal burns with clean running water for a minimum of ten minutes, ideally twenty, and the British Red Cross says to cool for at least twenty minutes.

First make the scene safe and remove the person from the source of the burn. If there is no running water IFRC says any cold liquid, such as juice or milk, will work. It says not to use ice-cold water, because that can cause hypothermia, especially in children and with large burns, and not to apply ice.

afterFigure.text: Take care with children who are being cooled, and watch for signs that they are getting too cold.

lead.text: Take off clothing and jewellery on or near the burn, unless they are stuck to the skin, because jewellery is hard to remove once swelling starts. After cooling, IFRC says to use a moisture-keeping, non-stick dressing such as hydrogel, and the British Red Cross says to cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.

IFRC says to call the emergency number if the burn is large, deep or near the face, mouth, throat or genital area, or if it was caused by chemicals, electricity or flames. It says to seek medical advice for a baby or vulnerable person, and the British Red Cross says always for a child.

reveal.text: Cold liquids such as milk or juice are accepted when there is no running water, but ice is not.
Ice, butter, cream, toothpaste, plasters and burst blisters are all on the list of things not to do.

steps.headline: A child pulls a cup of hot tea onto their arm.

workedSteps.text: Move the child from the source and make sure the area is safe, then take off wet clothing that is not stuck.
Hold the arm under cool running water, aiming at least ten minutes and ideally twenty, and call for medical advice because it is a child.
After cooling, cover the burn loosely with the clear wrap that the British Red Cross names.
Watch the child for signs of getting too cold while they were being cooled.

lead.text: For chemical burns on the skin or in the eyes, IFRC says to rinse with running water until the pain eases, avoid direct contact with the chemical yourself and take care that the diluted chemical does not touch healthy tissue. For an eye, remove contact lenses, rinse with clean running water or sterile saline, and avoid contaminating the other eye. IFRC says that if a chemical is swallowed you do not try to dilute it, and you contact the poison centre or the emergency service. A person with a chemical burn to the eye should not drive.
A burn from electricity or from flames is on IFRC's list for calling the emergency number. Make the scene safe first, because exposed wires are a danger to you as well.

reveal.text: Running water works for a chemical burn as it does for a thermal one, but the aim is to wash the chemical away.

Cooling needs no special equipment, only running water or, failing that, any cold liquid, so anyone can start it straight away.

blocks.text: You saw that IFRC and the British Red Cross differ on the minimum but agree on twenty minutes, that ice, butter and burst blisters are avoided, and that large, deep, facial, chemical, electrical and flame burns need the emergency number.

lessons.title: Fractures, sprains and dislocations
lessons.orientation: Support a suspected fracture and say which injuries need urgent help.

reveal.text: The next screen explains why any injured limb is treated as a possible break.

lead.text: IFRC's key action for fractures, sprains and strains is to keep the injury still to reduce pain. A **fracture** is a broken bone, and the signs are swelling, bruising, deformity, pain and difficulty moving the limb, a limb that looks shortened or twisted, and sometimes a snap or a grating sensation. A **sprain** or **strain** is an injury to a ligament or muscle. First aiders are not expected to diagnose which it is: IFRC says the only accurate way is with an X-ray, and that when in doubt you assume a fracture.

The British Red Cross agrees and adds that a person who can still move the limb may nonetheless have a break. A **dislocation**, where a bone is out of its joint, is treated as a fracture, and the British Red Cross says never to try to put it back.

IFRC says to help the person keep the injury still, support it in a comfortable position, and keep the limb elevated if that reduces swelling. The British Red Cross says to support the limb above and below the injury with the person's own hand, a cushion or clothing. A sling and bandages can hold it, as in the figure. You support it as you find it. IFRC says straightening an angled limb is for trained people in remote places, when the limb below the break is cool or pale, or splinting is not possible.

IFRC says that cold on a closed injury may reduce pain, if applied soon after the injury, for up to 20 consecutive minutes, wrapped in a cloth. It also says to record the time of the injury, as that helps professionals compare the injured limb with the healthy one.

afterFigure.text: If the person has to be moved over bumpy ground, IFRC says to splint the limb in a way that limits pain and allows safe transport.

diagram.alt: Three drawings of a person with an injured arm. In the first, the arm is padded with cushions above and below the injury in the position it was found. In the second, a forearm rests in a triangular sling across the body. In the third, a cold pack wrapped in cloth is on the forearm.

reveal.text: The skin can be damaged by cold, so the pack goes in a cloth, and cooling stops if it is too painful.

steps.headline: A fall on an outstretched hand leaves a swollen, deformed wrist.

workedSteps.text: You help the person keep the wrist still and avoid trying to straighten it.
You support it in the position in which you ___ it, using a sling and padding.
You apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes and ask the person to rest.
You call the emergency number if there is a great deal of pain or swelling, signs of shock or an abnormal limb position, and record the time of injury.

lead.text: IFRC says to call the emergency service if the person has a lot of pain or swelling, signs of shock, a break of the thigh bone or a limb in an abnormal position. Bleeding inside a long bone such as the thigh can itself be life threatening. If a wound is present and bone may be showing, the priority is to stop the bleeding and limit infection, stabilise the limb as for any fracture and treat for shock.

A suspected pelvic fracture, which IFRC links with spine injury, is managed by helping the person lie flat, padding between the legs and binding them together at the knees and feet, and not rocking the pelvis.

blocks.text: A fall on an outstretched hand can leave a wrist swollen, bruised and painful, and IFRC states that first aid providers are not expected to tell a broken bone from an injured ligament, since the only accurate way to do so is with an X-ray.
The guidance is therefore written for an injury whose nature you do not know, and its key action is the same whatever the injury turns out to be: keep the injured part still, which reduces pain.

lessons.title: Head and spine injury
lessons.orientation: Recognise a concussion and its warning signs, and keep a person still when a spine injury is suspected.

lead.text: A **concussion** is a common type of head injury that follows a forceful bump, blow or jolt to the head or body, and the British Red Cross describes it as the brain being shaken inside the skull. IFRC suggests three questions: did a potential injury occur, was the mechanism one that could injure the head, and was there any altered mental status. If all three answers are yes, the person is removed from the activity and either the emergency service is called or they are sent to a qualified health professional.

If the blow caused only a bump, a mild headache or nausea, the person can rest and be watched. IFRC says that a person with none of the warning signs may carry on with their day but should be observed for 24 hours, since signs can develop later. Guidance differs a little here: the British Red Cross says to call for emergency help if you suspect concussion, and IFRC lists the warning signs that call for it.

reveal.text: The next screen gives IFRC's complete list of warning signs.

lead.text: The figure lists the signs on which IFRC says emergency care should be accessed immediately after a blow to the head, among them becoming unresponsive even for a few seconds, a seizure, and vomiting more than once.

IFRC says that the main thing to look for is a change in the person, such as a child being very quiet and stopping play, and that these signs can appear straight away or over several hours or days. The British Red Cross says that someone who played sport must not return until seen by a professional.

steps.headline: A cyclist falls and is briefly confused, but walks. Twenty minutes later she is drowsy and vomits.

workedSteps.text: The fall and the confusion mean a head injury is possible, so she is made to rest and is watched.
Twenty minutes later she vomits, and IFRC counts vomiting as a warning sign once it happens more than a certain number of times.
She is also drowsy, which is a change in her behaviour. Together these are warning signs.
You call the emergency number and keep her head and neck still while you monitor her response and breathing until help arrives.

lead.text: Suspect a spine injury after a fall from a height greater than standing, a road collision, or a dive into shallow water, and when there is neck or back pain, tingling, weakness or an obvious deformity. IFRC says to access the emergency service whenever a spine injury is suspected. An alert person should keep as still as possible, and one who is less alert may need their head gently supported. IFRC says not to apply a cervical collar, a rigid brace fitted around the neck, and not to strap the person's head or neck.

If the person is unresponsive but breathing normally, IFRC says to leave them as found, keep the airway open with head tilt and chin lift or with a jaw thrust, which may move the neck less, and call. The British Red Cross says to turn them onto their side anyway, keeping the spine straight and getting help if possible. If breathing is not normal, both sources start CPR, since breathing comes before the spine.

Keeping the person still is the first aid, and the next move is to call.

lead.text: IFRC says that if the person must be moved, for example because of danger, it is best done by at least two first aid providers, with one keeping the person's head in line with their spine. A person who is unresponsive and breathing normally with suspected spine injury should otherwise be moved only when emergency help arrives or when they are in harm's way.
Head injury and spine injury often go together, and IFRC says that each should be considered when the other is suspected.

blocks.text: IFRC says a concussion can be difficult to identify, because the signs vary, do not always appear immediately, and some people do not recognise or admit to them. The guidance therefore works by watching for change in the person, and it lists the signs that mean the emergency service should be called.
A suspected spine injury has a rule of its own, which is to keep the person as still as possible and call the emergency service.

blocks.text: You saw that the warning signs include brief unresponsiveness, repeated vomiting, a severe headache of over two hours and fluid from the nose or ears, and that the British Red Cross is stricter than IFRC about calling for suspected concussion.
For a spine injury both sources keep the person still, differ on an unresponsive person who is breathing, and agree that CPR comes first if breathing is not normal.

lessons.title: Heart attack and stroke
lessons.orientation: Tell a heart attack from a stroke and give first aid for each.

lead.text: A **heart attack** is usually caused by a blockage in one of the vessels supplying the heart muscle, which damages the heart. IFRC says the chest pain may be described as discomfort, pressure, squeezing or burning, and may spread to the arm, shoulder, jaw or back, with sweating, shortness of breath or paleness. A heart attack can start with vague complaints, especially in women, older people and people with diabetes: nausea, breathlessness, pain between the shoulder blades or in the upper abdomen.

IFRC distinguishes a heart attack from **angina**, where the pain is often familiar and eases with rest and the person's medication, while the pain of a heart attack is often more persistent. Heart attacks are often mistaken for indigestion, so IFRC says to call if the pain persists after indigestion medicine.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the full first aid steps and the difference from a cardiac arrest.

steps.headline: First aid for a heart attack

lead.text: IFRC says to call the emergency number immediately if you suspect a heart attack, even if the pain has lasted only a couple of minutes, to help the person sit in a comfortable position and to ask a bystander to bring a defibrillator if one is available. If the person has their own medicine for angina, help them take it.

IFRC says you may suggest that an adult chews aspirin, unless they are allergic to it, have a bleeding disorder or have already taken the recommended dose. The figures differ between sources: IFRC gives 150 to 500 mg, and the British Red Cross says no more than 300 mg in one dose, so follow the guidance of your own country. If the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, a heart attack has become a cardiac arrest, and CPR and the AED follow, as in the figure.

lead.text: A **stroke** happens when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blockage or by bleeding. IFRC says that first aid providers should use a stroke assessment system and recommends FAST, whose letters stand for Face, Arm, Speech and Time, as the figure shows. Time is the cue to call the emergency number at once and note when the symptoms began.

Other signs include sudden numbness or weakness on one side, confusion, trouble seeing or walking, a sudden severe headache and a seizure in someone who does not have epilepsy. IFRC says that mild symptoms lasting only a few minutes may be a transient ischaemic attack and still need prompt care, and that first aid providers should not give oxygen to a person who may have a stroke.

afterFigure.text: IFRC lists aspirin only in its guidance on chest pain, and neither IFRC nor the British Red Cross advises it for a stroke. Because a stroke can be caused by a bleed, as well as by a blockage, and you cannot tell which, you do not give it.

steps.headline: A woman's smile is crooked and her speech is slurred.

workedSteps.text: You ask her to smile and see that one corner of her mouth droops, which is a positive Face sign.
You ask her to raise both arms, and one drifts down, which is a positive Arm sign.
Her speech is slurred, which is a positive Speech sign. At the Time step, you ___ the emergency number at once and note when the symptoms began.
You help her into the most comfortable position, support her if she may fall, and keep talking to her while you monitor her breathing.

reveal.text: Each minute of delay costs brain tissue, so symptoms are never watched to see if they pass.

lead.text: People often wait to see whether symptoms pass, though for a stroke early medical care greatly improves the outcome. Many expect chest pain to be crushing, but symptoms can be subtle in women, older people and people with diabetes.
A person with a heart attack is awake and gets aspirin, if suitable, and rest. A person with a stroke gets the FAST check, a call and comfort, and no oxygen.

blocks.text: IFRC's 2025 edition added a clear definition of each term: a heart attack is a blockage in a vessel that supplies the heart muscle, and a cardiac arrest is when the heart stops pumping effectively. The two are connected, since a heart attack can lead to cardiac arrest, and what a first aider does is quite different for each.

A stroke, in which blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted, shows itself differently again. The guidance for both conditions is to call at once rather than wait to see whether the symptoms pass.

blocks.text: You saw that the signs of a heart attack can be subtle in women, older people and people with diabetes, that aspirin figures differ between IFRC and the British Red Cross, and that aspirin is not advised for a stroke.

lessons.title: Allergic reactions and poisoning
lessons.orientation: Recognise anaphylaxis, help with an auto-injector and respond to poisoning.

lead.text: IFRC says that a mild allergic reaction, such as red, itchy eyes, sneezing or hives, may progress unpredictably to a life-threatening one, called **anaphylaxis**, in minutes. In anaphylaxis there may be difficulty breathing or wheezing, swelling of the tongue and throat causing hoarseness or noisy breathing, and signs of shock such as pale or ashen skin, confusion and collapse. Difficulty swallowing is often the first symptom.

The person has usually met something they are allergic to, such as food, an insect sting, a medicine or latex, and they often know it and carry a prescribed **adrenaline auto-injector**. IFRC calls the medicine epinephrine, and the British Red Cross and the ERC call it adrenaline. It is the same drug.

reveal.text: The figure on the next screen shows the site, the pen and the position.

lead.text: IFRC says to call the emergency service as soon as you recognise a severe reaction, to help the person lie down or, if breathing is difficult, to sit, and to help them use their auto-injector. The best place for the injection is the middle of the outer side of the thigh, through clothing if it is not thick. The British Red Cross says to follow the instructions on the packaging, and to hand the used injector to the ambulance crew.

Whether a first aider may use the injector for someone else depends on local law. IFRC says that if there is no improvement within five to ten minutes, a second dose may be considered if the emergency service has not arrived. The dose is set by the prescribed device, and this course gives no dose.

afterFigure.text: Do not wait for a reaction to ease before using the injector. Because the person can worsen quickly, IFRC says to give it when the symptoms of anaphylaxis are present.

workedSteps.text: A teacher calls the emergency number as soon as the severe reaction is recognised.
The child has her own auto-injector. The teacher helps her sit, because breathing is hard.
The teacher gives the injection into the middle of the outer thigh, through her thin leggings. The guidance says it can go through ___ that is not thick.
The teacher keeps watching her breathing and response, tells the dispatcher that the injector was used and gives the used pen to the crew.

lead.text: IFRC's key action for poisoning is to identify the poison, the amount and the time, and to call a poison centre or the emergency service. First stop or limit further exposure, but only if it is safe for you, since a room with gas, such as carbon monoxide, is a danger to the rescuer. Follow the instructions of the poison centre, place the person on their left side if possible and watch their breathing.

IFRC says not to make the person vomit, as it may damage the throat, and the British Red Cross adds that a corrosive substance burns the throat again on the way up. The two sources differ a little about drinks: IFRC lets a responsive person rinse and spit out any poison in the mouth, and says to give no milk, water or charcoal unless the poison centre says so, and the British Red Cross says not to give anything to drink. If a chemical is on the skin or in the eye, rinse it with running water as for a chemical burn.

afterFigure.text: For some poisons, such as cyanide or corrosives, IFRC says to avoid rescue breaths and to give chest compressions only if CPR is needed.

diagram.alt: Two lists about poisoning. Do: stop the exposure if safe, find out the substance, amount and time, call, place the person on their left side, give containers to the crew. Do not: make them vomit, give drinks or charcoal unless told, dilute a swallowed chemical, or give rescue breaths for some poisons.

The container's label tells the professionals what the person swallowed, so you keep it.

lead.text: For a mild reaction IFRC says to ask about known allergies and prescribed medicine, remove the allergen if you can, for example by rinsing it off the skin, and help the person into a comfortable position. If allergy tablets are what the person usually takes, you can help with them.

The person is monitored closely, since a mild reaction can develop into a severe one. IFRC also says that a person who had a severe reaction should be monitored for the three days that follow, because the reaction may return.

lessons.nextAction: Recognise heat exhaustion, heat stroke and hypothermia, and give first aid for each, with bites and stings.

blocks.text: IFRC points out that a mild allergic reaction may progress unpredictably to life-threatening anaphylaxis in minutes, so the guidance is built around speed.
Poisoning calls for the same speed and a different kind of care, because what helps depends on what the substance was, how much was taken and when, and some well-meant actions make it worse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to recognise anaphylaxis, say how to help with an auto-injector and respond to poisoning without making it worse.
intro.whyItMatters: This lesson teaches the knowledge, not the hands-on skill, which comes from a course with an instructor. In a real emergency you call your local emergency number first.

recap.keyIdea: In anaphylaxis you call and help the person use their auto-injector in the outer thigh, and in poisoning you stop the exposure if safe, gather the facts, call, and never make the person vomit.

blocks.text: You saw that the auto-injector goes on the middle of the outer thigh through thin clothing, that a second dose can be considered after five to ten minutes, and that the person is monitored for three days. Poison advice differs a little between IFRC and the British Red Cross on drinks.
The medicine is named epinephrine or adrenaline depending on the country, and the dose is set by the device.

lessons.title: Heat, cold and bites
lessons.orientation: Tell heat exhaustion from heatstroke, treat hypothermia and respond to bites.

reveal.text: The next screen tells heatstroke from the milder heat exhaustion, and the one after it gives the cooling steps and a difference between the two sources.

lead.text: IFRC splits hyperthermia, in which the body cannot control its temperature, into a mild to moderate form, **heat exhaustion**, and a severe one, **heatstroke**. In heat exhaustion the skin is cool, pale and clammy, the person sweats heavily and may be thirsty, with headache, cramps, a rapid weak pulse and dizziness. In heatstroke the person has stopped sweating, the skin is hot, flushed and dry, the temperature is above 40 °C, and they may be confused, aggressive, drowsy or have a seizure.

If you are unsure, the British Red Cross says to help the person rest in a cool place and call the emergency number for advice. IFRC lists the signs that mean you call: unusual behaviour or confusion, a seizure, a temperature above 39 °C, stopped sweating, or being unable to drink without vomiting.

diagram.alt: Two lists comparing heat exhaustion and heatstroke by skin and sweat, body signs, mind, and what to do. Heat exhaustion: cool, pale, clammy skin and heavy sweating, alert, rest and cooling. Heatstroke: hot, flushed, dry skin with sweating stopped, confusion or seizure, call at once and cool quickly.
